description: Technetium 99m Neurolite interictal brain SPECT obtained for SISCOM analysis with previous technetium 99 Neurolite ictal brain SPECT. description:
CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring session due to the presence of independent multifocal bilateral epileptogenic abnormalities. During the monitoring session, the patient had one of his typical seizures with seizure onset in the left hemisphere. Ictal SPECT injection was done with this seizure. These findings would be consistent with the diagnosis of localization-related epilepsy. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged video EEG; Dysrhythmia gr. 3 independent multifocal bilateral spike and sharp waves, maximal left hemisphere; Recorded one seizure with seizure onset in the left hemisphere; Ictal SPECT injection; EKG monitor. REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring was for approximately 2 days. 

BACKGROUND: During the wake recording, there was 9-1 Hz alpha activity seen over the posterior head region. During sleep, there was normal symmetric sleep activity of V-waves, sleep spindles, and K-complexes. 

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: During the monitoring session, there was frequent activation of bilateral independent multifocal epileptogenic abnormalities, maximal over the left hemisphere. 

CLINICAL EVENTS: During the monitoring session, the patient had one of his typical seizures. This was at 09:07. During the seizure, the patient had behavior arrest and was staring off for a few minutes. On the EEG, the ictal onset was characterized by rhythmic theta discharges seen over the left hemisphere, maximal over the left frontotemporal head region. During the seizure, the patient was injected for ictal SPECT study. The time of injection as follows: seizure onset at 09:55:07, injection was at 09:56:15, and the end of the seizure was at 09:55:34.The EKG monitor was otherwise unremarkable.

description: MRI head without and with intravenous contrast utilizing seizure Protocol. Additional imaging with fiducial markers in place was also performed at the request of the referring physician. In comparison to the prior study, there is no significant interval change. Stable encephalomalacia with associated gliosis of the parieto-occipital region bilaterally is unchanged. Stable ex-vacuo dilatation of the atria of lateral ventricles, left greater than right. According to the clinical record, there is a history of prior trauma in this region. Previously noted increased FLAIR signal intensity of medial temporal lobes bilaterally is not seen on today's study. It is likely that the previously reported finding was artifactual in nature. Normal intracranial vessel flow-voids. No abnormal parenchymal or leptomeningeal enhancement. Interval development of mucosal thickening of maxillary sinuses bilaterally with probable mucus retention cyst. Stable probable mucus retention cyst of left sphenoid sinus. Remainder of study is unchanged.

description:
CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring session due to the presence of frequent independent left posterior temporo-occipital, left mesial temporal and left anterior temporal epileptiform discharges. During the monitoring session, the patient had four complex partial seizures. All of these seizures began in the posterior contacts of the left temporo-occipital grid. The findings would be consistent with a localization-related epilepsy with seizure onset in the left occipital neocortex. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG; Dysrhythmia gr. 3 independent left posterior temporo-occipital, left mesial temporal,
left anterior temporal spike and sharp waves; Recorded four. partial seizures of left occipital onset; EKG monitor. 

REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring was performed for approximately 2 days. Intracranial monitoring was performed using an 8-contact straight strip was inserted into the left frontal region parallel to the superior temporal gyrus with contact #1 oriented anteriorly (LFS). An 8x8 grid was inserted with contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly and contact #64 oriented superiorly and posteriorly over the left posterior temporo-occipital region (LTG). A 4-contact straight strip was inserted with contact #1 oriented anteriorly over the left anterior temporal pole (ATS). A 4-contact straight strip was inserted over the left inferior subtemporal region, posterior to the anterior temporal strip (ITS). A 4-contact orthogonal depth electrode was inserted between the anterior temporal strip and inferior subtemporal strip, targeting the hippocampus (AD). Posterior to the inferior temporal strip, there was another 4-contact orthogonal depth electrode targeting the hippocampus (PD). 

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: During the wake and sleep recordings, there were independent epileptiform discharges in the left posterior temporo-occipital grid, left mesial temporal depths, and left inferior subtemporal strip. Spike and sharp waves occurred in LTG contacts #1, 3, 4, 21, 22, 23, 25-28, 30-31, 38-40, 50-52, 57-60, and 63. Spikes and sharp waves were also present in ITS contacts #1 and 2, AD contacts #1 and 2, and PD contacts #1 and 2. 

CLINICAL EVENTS: During the monitoring session, the patient had four complex partial seizures with onset from the posterior contacts of the left posterior temporo-occipital grid. The dates and times of these events are as follows. Seizure #1 occurred 00:21:39 to 00:22:34. Clinically, the patient made a humming sound at 00:22:06 then had some chewing movement and postures with the left hand. At 00:21:39, the EEG showed paroxysmal fast activity on LTG contact #59 which then evolved into spike activities and LTG #58 and 59. Spike and wave discharges then spread to involve LTG #2, 10, 11, and 18, with subsequent involvement of LTG #50 and spread to the ATS contacts #3 and 4, AD contacts #1 and 2, and PD #2 and 4. Seizure #2 at 01:20:59 to 01:22:27. The clinical onset occurred after EEG onset. The patient moved the left arm up and fist with the left hand and postures and began humming. The EEG showed fast activity at LTG #59 at 01:20:59, which then evolves into spike activity in LTG #58 and 59. At 01:21:10, there was spread of spike and wave activity to LTG #2, 3, 10, 11, 18, and 19 with subsequent spread to the depth electrodes PD #1-4 and AD #1 and 2 as well as anterior temporal strip #3 and 4.Seizure #3 occurred at 04:45:07 to 04:46:39. There were rhymic left hand movements with clinical onset after EEG onset. The EEG pattern was identical to seizures #1 and 2. Seizure #4 occurred at 21:04:47 to 21:05:53. Clinically, the patient aroused from sleep, hummed, and had language difficulty and does not answer questions and continues to have difficulty speaking after the electrographic seizure. The EEG onset and evolution was identical to seizures #1, 2, and 3.The EKG monitor was unremarkable.

description: CT head without IV contrast. Comparison with previous head MRI. New postoperative changes of left craniotomy with subdural grid placement about the left parietal lobe and about the temporal lobe anteriorly, posteriorly and laterally. Two depth electrodes are identified medial to the left temporal lobe, in the region of the hippocampus. The superior most electrodes are deviated slighly medially, presumably due to some subdural fluid, though this is obscured by streak artifact. 3 mm of cortical step-off at the craniotomy site. Small amount of PO pneumocephalus anterior to the left temporal and frontal lobes, and at the craniotomy site. Subcutaneous fluid, hemorrhage and air about the left calvarium. Partially visualized encephalomalacia within the parieto-occipital regions bilaterally. Associated local ex vacuo dilatation of the occipital horns of the lateral ventricles. Mucosal thickening and/or retention cysts throughout the visualized paranasal sinuses.

description: 1. Left temporal occipital craniotomy. 2. Placement of subdural grid electrodes. 3. Placement of hippocampal depth electrodes. The patient was brought to OR and placed under general endotracheal anesthesia. He was placed in Mayfield pinions set to 60 pounds of pressure and then positioned supine with a left shoulder bump and head turned far to the right. All pressure points were meticulously padded. The patient's fiducials were then registered to the Stealth system successfully. A U-shaped incision was then marked extending from the zygoma up towards the midline sagittal suture and back towards the occipital pole. This area was then prepped and draped in the standard sterile fashion. After pausing for correct patient, procedure, site, and antibiotic administration, the incision was infiltrated with a solution of 0.25% bupivacaine with epinephrine. A 15 blade was then used to score the epidermis along the previously marked incision. The incision was extended down to the bone using fine needlepoint cautery. The scalp flap was then reflected and secured in place with fish hooks. Next, a Midas drill with a perforator was obtained, and burr holes were placed in the zygoma, posteriorly and rostrally, lateral to the sagittal sinus. The bone flap was then turned with a footplate. During elevation of the bone flap, vigorous venous bleeding was encountered. The bleeding vessel was packed with Gelfoam and cottonoids. Pressure was also applied until hemostatic control was achieved. We then turned our attention towards completing the bone flap elevation. Following removal of the bone flap, the dura was then opened in a cruciate manner using a 15 blade and Jones scissors. The dura was reflected and tacked up with Vicryl sutures. After the dura was opened, Photography was called to take a picture of the exposure in a fixed position. Following this, subdural grid electrodes and depth electrodes were placed with the assistance of the Neurology Team. First, a single 8 x 8 subdural grid was placed over the left temporal-occipital region. Next, a 1 x 4 subdural grid was placed over the anterior temporal region followed by placement of a 1 x 4 grid along the inferior temporal region. In addition, a 1 x 8 grid was placed in the subfrontal region. This was followed by placement of an anterior depth electrode and a posterior depth electrode into the hippocampus. A 1 x 4 ground reference contact was also placed between the scalp and cavarium. Each of these grids were secured in place to dura using Vicryl sutures. Once again, Photography was called, and the position of these grids was documented. Each of the grid leads were then externalized through the scalp using a 14-gauge needle and angiocatheter and then attached to EEG monitoring. During externalization, it was noticed that the posterior depth electrode had pulled out. This depth electrode was reinserted without incidence. We again confirmed that all grids were functioning properly. Our attention was then turned to the dura. We approximated the dura with interrupted Vicryl sutures. The wound was then copiously irrigated with bacitracin irrigation. Following closure of the dura, the bone flap was then replaced with temporary silk stay sutures. The subgaleal layer was then closed using 2-0 Vicryl sutures. Finally, the skin was closed using a nylon baseball suture. Each of the grid leads that had been externalized were then sutured to the skin using 3-0 silk in a pursestring fashion. The patient was then taken out of his Mayfield pinions, and a sterile head wrap was placed. There were no complications during the procedure. The patient was awakened and taken to the spiral CT scanner for final confirmation of grid location. He was then taken to the Pediatric ICU for further recovery.

Upon completion of the resection of the occipital pole, we then irrigated the surgical site copiously with saline irrigation. We then proceeded to close the dura with a combination of primary closure and use of pericranium in those areas that were unable to be approximated primarily. The dura was sutured using 4-0 interrupted Vicryls and running 4-0 Vicryl sutures. The dura was then copiously irrigated. We then turned our attention to the section of the brain that had bled torrentially during the patient's first craniotomy. We removed the Gelfoam that had been placed there previously. Upon removal of the Gelfoam we again encountered significant amounts of bleeding. There appeared to be two dural veins that had come underneath the skull and scalloped it's surface. These bleeding vessels were packed with large amounts of Gelfoam and the Gelfoam anchored in place with Vicryl sutures. With pressure, we were able to bring the bleeding under control and obtain good hemostasis. We then irrigated the dura copiously with bacitracin irrigation. The bone flap was then replaced using four medium plates and screws. This field was once again irrigated copiously. The temporalis muscle was approximated using Vicryl sutures. The galea was then closed using 2-0 interrupted Vicryl sutures. Staples were used to close the skin. There were no complications during the surgery. The patient was awakened, extubated, and transferred to the PACU for further recovery without incident.

description:
Brain, left occipital lobe, resection: Cortex and underlying white matter with changes consistent with remote destructive injury. See comment. Comment: The cortex shows multiple areas of severe neuronal loss and gliosis associated with atrophy and focal dystrophic calcification. Calcifications are present focally in the meninges and vascular wall. An immunohistochemical stain was performed on paraffin-embedded tissue using antibodies to GFAP. GFAP highlights disruption of the normal cortical architecture, reactive gliosis and subpial gliosis. An immunohistochemical stain for NeuN immunostain highlights neurons. 

GROSS DESCRIPTION: Received fresh labeled "left occipital brain lobe" is a 7.51 gram, 5.2 x 2.8 x 0.8 cm portion of brain. The specimen is sent in formalin to the neuropathology working group for sectioning.
